definition: Placed lower than a charge or ordinary would ordinarily appear on a shield.
An alleged dishonourable alteration described in later heraldic manuals; systematic historical use is disputed.
Accompanied by another figure on each side of the principal charge.
The complete heraldic display around an armiger's shield, potentially including a helm, crest, mantling, supporters and motto.
The nut of an oak tree, sometimes represented within its cup.
Back to back, especially of a pair of animals or birds.
An Akan system of visual symbols associated with sayings, histories and social meaning, particularly in textiles and related media; not automatically equivalent to European heraldry.
Facing the viewer directly rather than shown in profile.
Arms referring to a bearer's name, profession or qualities through imagery.
A stylized ship's anchor used as a heraldic charge.
A ring-shaped heraldic figure; distinguish its use as an inscribed ring from the smaller annulet.
A metalworking implement shown as a charge in craft and personal arms.
The identifying reference assigned to an object or collection by an archive.
The metal silver, commonly represented as white.
Spanish term for canting arms, referring to a pun or verbal allusion to the bearer's name. Portuguese normally uses *armas falantes*.
Describes claws, horns or other natural weapons, often when separately tinctured.
French term for canting arms, involving a pictorial pun or allusion.
A person, family, or institution associated with the use of arms; entitlement and inheritance require inquiry into the governing heraldic tradition and evidence.
French term for armorial bearings, whose scope varies with context.
A collection or register of coats of arms; also an adjective relating to arms.
A formal expression for arms, sometimes referring to the whole heraldic achievement.
French expression for a general armorial register or compilation.
A handwritten or illustrated source containing descriptions or pictures of arms.
An index arranged by designs or charges rather than primarily by bearers' names.
A compilation of coats of arms prepared for identification, record or display.
A seal displaying an armorial device, which may preserve evidence of historical use.
The heraldic device, especially the design displayed on the shield.
A joint display associating the armorial identities of spouses or families.
Arms representing a realm, sovereign authority or a ruler's office.
An inescutcheon conveying a particular hereditary or marital claim in some traditions.
A pointed missile, with feathers and orientation optionally specified.
Adopting an armorial design without receiving a new official grant.
Having antlers, especially when these are separately tinctured from the stag.
An addition authorized in recognition of distinction or service.
The heraldic colour blue. Its exact shade is not universally fixed.
A distinctive heraldic emblem that may be used separately from the shield or crest.
A flag whose whole field displays an armorial design, rather than a logo on a shield.
A narrow horizontal stripe; multiple bars are commonly shown together.
Two narrow parallel horizontal bars treated together as a heraldic figure.
A narrow horizontal band following a serpentine or sinuously curved course, as specified in the blazon.
Having arrow points or the outer green parts of a rose specifically represented.
A very narrow horizontal stripe, smaller than an ordinary bar.
Divided into an even number of alternating horizontal stripes.
Divided into alternating horizontal bands whose partition lines undulate.
The lower portion of the shield.
Of a bird, having a beak of a particular tincture.
A diagonal ordinary running from the bearer's dexter chief to sinister base.
A diagonal ordinary running from sinister chief to dexter base.
A narrow diagonal ordinary of the same orientation as a bend.
A narrow diagonal stripe following the direction of a bend sinister.
Divided into repeating diagonal bands along the direction of a bend.
Divided into repeating diagonal bands following a bend sinister.
Indicates a principal charge accompanied by other charges on either side or around it.
In conventional English blazon, a roundel Or (gold). Other systems may name roundels by their tincture instead of using the specialized English vocabulary.
A small rectangular heraldic charge.
French expression for the wording or process of formally describing arms.
French archival expression for painted or coloured armorial representations; the phrase can designate a manuscript series rather than grants.
A formal verbal description of arms, written according to heraldic conventions.
The process and conventions of formally describing heraldic designs.
A light sky-blue tincture recognized in some heraldic vocabularies; not identical to every rendering of Azure.
A wild pig used as a heraldic animal charge.
The head of a wild pig, sometimes shown couped or erased.
A band following the outer perimeter of a shield.
Portuguese term for a coat of arms.
A named buff-coloured tincture occurring in certain modern Canadian and United States military heraldic contexts; its exact formal use is source-specific.
German term for a non-noble family's arms, distinct from civic arms.
Heraldic arms of non-noble townspeople or families, especially in central Europe.
Arms borne by a non-noble family in a German-speaking context; not necessarily the official arms of a municipality.
An animal's head shown looking straight outward without the neck.
A system of distinguishing members of a family by differences in their arms.
A younger family line potentially distinguished by a mark of difference.
A four-pointed anti-cavalry device depicted with a spike upward.
Canada's official authority for granting, recording and registering heraldic emblems.
Arms containing a visual pun or reference to the bearer's name.
A square or rectangular figure placed in an upper corner of the shield, usually dexter chief.
A ceremonial cap often depicted with a crimson crown and an ermine lining.
A flesh-coloured tincture used in some heraldic systems.
A fortified building charge with towers, battlements and sometimes a doorway.
A descriptive record that identifies a source but does not prove it was examined.
An uncommon grey tincture, distinct from the seven principal tinctures.
A hat-like heraldic item, sometimes meaning the cap of maintenance.
Any figure or emblem placed on a field or other heraldic figure.
A repeating pattern of adjacent squares alternating between two tinctures.
An ordinary in the shape of an inverted V.
A comparatively narrow chevron, sometimes shown in multiples.
Divided into repeated chevron-shaped bands of alternating tinctures.
Both the upper part of a shield and a horizontal ordinary occupying that part.
Italian word for a heraldic crest above a helmet.
A stylized five-lobed or five-petalled flower-like figure.
Arms identifying a town, city, county or other public territorial body.
Of a bird, shown with its wings folded against its body.
A heraldic design identifying a bearer or claimed bearer, represented by a blazon or emblazonment; whether a particular person is legally or customarily entitled to bear it is a separate question.
A legendary beast combining cockerel and reptilian features.
The study of the physical construction and history of manuscript books.
A ceremonial collar or chain of an order shown around a coat of arms.
Comparison of textual witnesses to identify differences between copies.
Name shared by distinct institutions, including the English College of Arms in London and Kenya's statutory College of Arms. Their jurisdictions and functions are not interchangeable.
The ground or base upon which supporters may stand beneath an achievement.
Composed of a single row of adjoining pieces in alternating tinctures.
A formal recognition of existing arms, different from creating new arms.
Joined or touching, with the nature of the connection dependent on context.
Turned toward sinister, especially of an animal ordinarily depicted facing dexter; French-derived usage also occurs in Canadian blazons.
Facing sinister instead of the direction conventionally expected.

A named copper-coloured tincture used in some modern heraldic grants, including Canadian arms; do not treat it as universally recognized or assume its position in a metal/colour rule without checking the design.
A small crown-like emblem whose particular form may convey rank.
Arms of an organization such as a university, charity or corporation.
Reclining with the body at rest and the head usually raised.
Composed of two adjoining rows of alternating small squares or rectangles.
A reverse ermine pattern, usually white ermine spots on black.
A potent fur pattern with rows of crutch-shaped figures arranged in opposing orientation.
Vair with adjoining rows of bell-shaped pieces set base to base.
A design in which colours and/or metals of charges reverse across a divided field.
A separate seal impressed on the back of a principal seal or attached arrangement; it is not necessarily on the reverse of the written document itself.
Severed cleanly along a smooth or straight boundary.
Running, generally with the animal's legs stretched out.
The Scottish heraldic court responsible for heraldic matters under Scots law.
A curved moon-shaped charge whose horns commonly point upward.
The heraldic device positioned atop the helmet, not the entire coat of arms.
A scholarly text with documented witnesses, variants and editorial choices.
An upright cross used as an ordinary or as a smaller charge.
A small cross with a crossing element near the end of each arm.
A cross with arms terminating in stylized fleurs-de-lis.
A cross whose arms expand toward their ends.
A cross with ends resembling the split ends of a millrind.
A cross with arms broadening outward, found in many regional forms.
A cross with short transverse bars at the ends of its arms.
A heraldic representation of sovereignty or authority, with meaning dependent on context.
A zigzag edge with comparatively large triangular teeth, as opposed to fine indented work.
The upper or front half of a wild boar, used as a charge or crest element.
The upper half of a lion, often used in crests or as a charge.
The right side from the bearer's perspective; the viewer's left.
The lower corner on the bearer's right, appearing at the viewer's lower left.
The upper corner on the bearer's right, appearing at the viewer's upper left.
A modification of arms to distinguish another bearer or branch.
Modifying arms to distinguish branches or individual bearers.
An old form of marshalling that combines parts of two coats of arms.
Historical study of documents, their form, authenticity and transmission.
An attitude of a bird, particularly an eagle, with wings spread.
Sleeping, shown at rest with the head typically lowered.
An eagle represented with two heads, common in several imperial traditions.
A partition line resembling the interlocking dovetail joints of carpentry.
A large heraldic bird, commonly displayed with its wings spread.
Armorial traditions of religious officeholders and institutions.
Raised, especially describing a bird's wings.
An edge formed like battlements, with repeated raised portions and gaps.
Curved or bent, especially of a human arm or an animal's body.
Passed through a ring, wreath or comparable surrounding object.
Describes a line or edge with a series of small curved indentations.
Placed higher on the shield than the customary position of a charge or ordinary.
Surmounted by an emblem or dignity such as a crown.
Torn or separated along an irregular jagged boundary.
Czech or Slovak term used for a coat of arms.
Standing upright rather than lying in the customary orientation.
A heraldic fur, conventionally white with black ermine-tail spots.
A reversed ermine fur, generally black with white ermine-tail spots.
An ermine variant with red details added to the conventional black spots on white.
A fur of black ermine spots scattered over a gold field.
A stylized scallop-shell charge.
A radiating heraldic figure derived from metal reinforcement on early shields.
Spanish for coat of arms or armorial shield depending on context.
A shield bearing arms; a small shield charge can be called an inescutcheon.
A star-like heraldic charge often shown with wavy rays.
A visual reproduction of a document or image, potentially preserving fine detail.
A horizontal ordinary across the centre of a shield.
Set in the horizontal direction of a fess, as opposed to upright or diagonally arranged.
A stylized fastening or shackle, especially familiar as an English badge.
The background surface of a shield, whether plain or divided.
A narrow band, especially a narrow chief in some English descriptive conventions.
A narrow contrasting border applied to a heraldic figure, particularly in flags.
Ending in a point, especially of the lower limb of a cross.
A pair of curved figures extending inward from the opposite sides of a shield.
A stylized floral charge associated with several European heraldic traditions.
A conventional variant spelling of fleur-de-lis, denoting the same stylized floral charge.
Alternately decorated with fleur-de-lis motifs on the two sides of a figure, notably a Scottish double tressure.
One leaf of a manuscript book, with a front and reverse side.
An interlaced geometric charge conventionally formed by a mascle and a saltire.
Covered with repeated interlaced diagonal strips in an open lattice pattern.
Bearing fruit of a specified tincture.
A category of heraldic patterned tinctures including ermine and vair.
An elongated lozenge, narrower and more pointed than a conventional diamond.
Divided into a repeating pattern of elongated diamond-shaped pieces.
A ship or boat with oars or sails shown as a heraldic charge; details vary by artistic and regional convention.
A bound sheaf of grain, often wheat.
The senior English King of Arms at the College of Arms.
Shown wearing an armoured glove or gauntlet, commonly describing a heraldic arm.
A banner with hanging tails, sometimes used as a charge.
Of an animal, wearing a collar or other device encircling the neck.
An official act creating armorial bearings by a competent heraldic authority.
A creature combining the foreparts of an eagle with the hindquarters of a lion.
An attitude in which an animal's head faces the viewer.
The heraldic colour red, one of the principal colours used in armorial design.
A triangular sector, often one of the pieces of a gyronny field.
A division of the field into triangular sectors radiating from a common point.
A stringed instrument used as a heraldic charge.
A scheme of dots and lines by which engravers represent heraldic tinctures without using coloured pigment; the Petra Sancta system became widely influential.
A funerary heraldic display, often diamond-shaped, with conventions indicating family status.
Of a fish, swimming upright with its head toward chief.
A helmet shown above the shield as part of a heraldic achievement.
An officer or specialist associated with armory, genealogy, and ceremonial protocol.
An institution or officer empowered under a defined system to administer arms.
A woman through whom paternal arms may pass as quarterings under certain inheritance rules.
An entry in a heraldic register, whose legal effect depends on the system involved.
An official inquiry into pedigrees and arms, prominent in early modern England.
The study, practice and administration of coats of arms and related devices.
Polish for a coat of arms, often a named design borne by several noble families.
Polish term for an armorial reference book, often compiled long after the events described.
Arms transmitted by descent under a relevant legal or customary system.
A reference point above the centre of a shield used for locating charges.
An equine charge represented in various attitudes.
A geometric personal, household or merchant sign sometimes used on seals, property or trade objects, with particular contexts of ownership and transmission.
A manuscript embellished with painting, ornamental work or precious metals.
Combining two armorial identities side by side in one shield.
Separate charges arranged diagonally along the line of a bend.
In the upper region of the shield rather than on a chief ordinary, unless the wording explicitly says otherwise.
Separate charges arranged horizontally across the field.
A group of separate charges following the inside perimeter of the shield.
Separate charges arranged one above another along a vertical line.
Shown on an inescutcheon to represent a heraldic claim under certain conventions.
Separate charges arranged in the shape of a diagonal cross.
An edge consisting of repeated small angular zigzags.
A smaller shield borne as a charge on a larger shield.
Woven over and under one another, such as rings or knots.
An edge formed of curved arcs oriented opposite to those of an engrailed line.
Turned upside down from the usual heraldic orientation.
Appearing to emerge from another figure or partition.
Japanese family or house emblem associated with mon traditions, not equivalent to European armorial law.
A key, with its ward, bow and orientation sometimes specified.
A senior rank of heraldic officer with jurisdiction-specific responsibilities.
Polish heraldic term for a crest, though the general word can mean a jewel.
A horizontal cadency mark with pendent points; traditionally linked to an eldest son in English usage.
Another word for the decorative mantling flowing from a heraldic helm.
Having a tongue of a specified tincture.
An official instrument used by certain heraldic authorities to document a grant of arms.
A heavily stylized feline charge appearing in many attitudes.
A heraldic lion shown walking, normally with one forepaw raised.
A lion rearing upright on one hind leg.
Scotland's principal heraldic officer with judicial and administrative responsibilities.
A diamond-shaped heraldic figure or alternative support used for some armorial displays.
Divided into a repeating pattern of diamond-shaped areas of alternating tinctures.
A pike fish shown as a heraldic charge, sometimes used as a visual pun on the name Lucy.
A conventionalized ship, especially familiar in Scottish and island arms.
Decorative representation of cloth issuing from a helmet, often flowing around a shield.
An individual surviving source attesting a text or design.
The leaf of a maple tree, frequently used in Canadian heraldry and civic symbolism.
Rules and methods for combining two or more coats of arms in a display.
A heraldic bird conventionally represented without visible feet in many European traditions. Some drawings vary; the term is not a species-level zoological identification.
A lozenge-shaped figure with a similarly shaped opening in its centre.
Marked with visible joints between stones or bricks, especially on walls, towers and crowns.
A documented chain of an artefact's creation, ownership and custody.
Formal recording of arms, particularly the Scottish process for a bearer or cadet branch.
Having limbs or legs of a specified tincture, especially of birds.
A stylized French heraldic bird often represented without beak or feet; compare the English martlet.
Czech expression for the arms or emblem of a town.

A heraldic class conventionally comprising Or and Argent. Some modern granting authorities also recognize additional named tinctures such as Copper or Buff, whose role must be evaluated in their own compositions.
An iron fitting associated with a millstone, rendered as a geometric charge.
A Japanese emblem used to identify households or organizations outside European armorial frameworks.
A Japanese family emblem, with its own history and rules of use.
A phrase associated with an armiger, often displayed on a scroll; its status varies by tradition.
A star-shaped heraldic charge, often five-pointed in English usage.
A crown formed with masonry and battlements, frequently associated with civic or corporate heraldry.
Of a fish, swimming horizontally.
Rising or emerging from behind an ordinary or division, with the upper part of a charge visible. Distinguish from issuant, which can describe a charge issuing from a line or other feature.
An edge or partition formed of repeated cloud-like curved lobes.
A reference point below the centre of a heraldic shield, toward its base.
The leaf of an oak tree, used individually or with branches and acorns.
The heraldic metal gold, often represented as yellow.
A principal geometric figure such as a fess, pale, bend or chevron.
A narrow border-like ordinary that follows the outline of a shield inside its field.
A long plume frequently used in crests and badges.
A charge depicted across and visually over other figures.
Study of historical handwriting and scripts used to read and date sources.
A vertical ordinary running from the top toward the base of a shield.
Oriented vertically in the manner of a pale rather than horizontally or diagonally.
A Y-shaped ordinary formed by three bands meeting at one point, found in some civic and personal arms.
A relatively narrow vertical stripe, sometimes appearing in multiple groups.
Divided into an even number of alternating vertical stripes.
Divided by both vertical and diagonal lines, forming a repeated geometric pattern.
Walking; an animal attitude, often used of lions.
Walking while the head faces the viewer.
Walking with the head turned backward.
A fur with gold ermine spots on a black field.
A winged horse of classical mythology, found as a heraldic charge, crest or supporter.
A black roundel in traditional English heraldic terminology.
A tapering medieval flag associated with a knight or mounted retinue.
A division of the field diagonally along the line of a bend.
Divided diagonally from sinister chief toward dexter base.
A division along the line of a chevron.
A horizontal division of the field.
A vertical division of the field.
Divided into three areas by lines meeting in the shape of a Y or its inverse.
Divided into four triangular areas by diagonal lines forming an X.
A historically influential scheme for representing heraldic tinctures with engraved patterns, popularized in the seventeenth century.
Having an opening revealing the underlying field.
A wedge-shaped heraldic figure, usually pointing down from the chief.
A silver or white roundel in conventional English heraldic terminology.
A lattice gate with chains used as a heraldic device.
A stylized fur pattern built from repeated crutch-shaped pieces, often blue and white.
A partition line with repeated projections resembling the heads of heraldic crutches.
Depicted in a charge's natural or conventionally natural colours rather than a named tincture.
An official or formally maintained collection of recorded arms.
The heraldic colour purple.
A junior heraldic officer, below a herald in several traditional hierarchies.
Of a cross, having a square enlargement or other square central portion, as specified in a blazon.
A substantial square or rectangular area placed in one corner of a shield.
Combining different arms in separate quarters of the same shield.
The division of a field into four quarters, or an arrangement of multiple armorial identities.
A stylized four-lobed floral or leaf-like figure.
An edge with short angular projections resembling the stumps of lopped branches.
Rearing up; a common attitude of a lion and some other beasts.
An insignia signifying an office or rank, notably embroidered East Asian civil and military badges; species, count, period and local rules matter.
The front side of a manuscript leaf, often abbreviated 'r'.
A named earthy red used in modern armorial practice, including South African descriptions; consult the particular grant for its role.
With the head turned backward over the shoulder.
Recording arms in a register, not always a legal act of granting arms.
Administrative entry of pre-existing arms, distinct from creating the design by a new grant.
A further registration or matriculation of inherited arms, especially in Scottish practice.
Legal or custodial conditions governing reuse of an image or textual reproduction.
Of two creatures, facing toward one another.
Polish expression for a heraldic clan or armorial group, not proof of shared descent.
A compiled display or list of armorial bearings, often dating from medieval practice.
A conventional heraldic flower, often shown with five petals.
A circular charge, sometimes named more specifically by its tincture.
Armorial bearings representing a sovereign or monarchy, rather than necessarily private arms.
An introductory contrast convention discouraging colour-on-colour and metal-on-metal placement, subject to exceptions.
The heraldic colour black.
Leaping or springing, with the forelegs raised.
A diagonal X-shaped cross, as an ordinary or charge.
An uncommon dark red tincture, classed as a stain by some heraldic writers.
A recognizable pattern or style of handwriting used in manuscript attribution.
A ribbon-like device carrying a motto or other inscription.
An engraved object used to impress a seal in wax or another material.
A single-edged blade or short sword, often associated with Saxon material culture and certain civic achievements; its distinctive curved knife form should not be confused with a generic sword.
Having the centre or seed of a heraldic flower separately described.
Sitting with the haunches on the ground.
Sitting while holding the forequarters upright.
Strewn with repeated small charges over a field.
Following a sinuous or winding outline, used for a partition or ordinary and not necessarily identical to a conventional wavy line.
A three-leaved clover or trefoil associated especially with Ireland, used as a heraldic charge.
The scholarly study of seals, their inscriptions, images, production and use.
The bearer's left, appearing on the viewer's right.
The lower corner on the bearer's left, appearing at the viewer's lower right.
The upper corner on the bearer's left, appearing at the viewer's upper right.
Of a plant or flower, shown with a short stem.
Recording precisely which evidence supports each historical claim.
A small branch or spray bearing leaves, flowers or fruit of a stated kind.
German word for a town's or city's arms.
A male deer with antlers used as a heraldic animal.
The head of a male deer, sometimes depicted caboshed, couped or erased.
A category used by some writers for additional tinctures; its contents are not universal.
A long flag historically displaying heraldic colours, badges or a motto.
Standing on all available feet.
Italian for a coat of arms or emblem, including personal and civic usage.
Italian expression for civic or municipal arms.
A smaller conventional geometric figure, such as an orle or canton.
Finnish for family arms, distinct from civic or state bearings.
Figures supporting or flanking the shield, governed by differing entitlements and customs.
A garment worn over armour that could display armorial devices.
Historical Polish nobility, with distinctive social and armorial traditions.
An armorial garment worn by a herald to signify the sovereign or office represented.
A mark or sign used in various Eurasian systems of identity, authority or ownership. Its history should not be collapsed into the hereditary western coat-of-arms system.
A handled drinking vessel shown as a heraldic charge, sometimes employed in canting arms.
A cross in the shape of the capital letter T, sometimes associated with Saint Anthony.
An uncommon orange-brown stain or tincture whose depiction differs among authorities.
A prickly flowering plant associated with Scottish symbolism.
Divided into three portions, with the direction or geometry specified by the blazon.
A heraldic colour, metal, or fur.
A twisted cloth wreath placed over the helm and beneath the crest.
A written rendering of an original document, distinct from translation.
A three-lobed plant-like charge resembling a clover leaf.
A narrow border set inside the field and following the outline of the shield.
A highly structured Ottoman calligraphic insignia naming a ruler and carrying formulaic strokes and curves; used in official and other contexts.
A traditional alternative term for a gently waving heraldic partition line.
Having the hooves of a specified tincture.
A mythical one-horned creature, often shown with distinctive heraldic features.
Finnish word for coat of arms, used in several compound expressions.
A stylized heraldic fur with recurring bell-shaped pieces, commonly alternating blue and white.

A rearrangement of the pieces of vair in which neighboring rows are aligned differently from ordinary vair; compare the tips and bases in the actual depiction rather than assuming point-to-point alignment.
A variation of vair arranged with the recurring shapes in vertical columns.
Of a human arm, wearing armour for the forearm, especially a vambrace.
Swedish word for heraldic arms, depending on context.
Swedish term for an armorial document, whose authority must be assessed historically.
Swedish term for a heraldic shield.
Textual differences between separate manuscripts or editions.
The reverse side of a manuscript leaf, often abbreviated 'v'.
The heraldic colour green.
An examination and recording of pedigrees and arms by authorized heraldic officers.
Of a charge, represented mainly as an outline through which its background remains visible.
Flying, used particularly of a bird with extended wings.
Shown wounded, usually with visible blood.
Dutch term for a description of heraldic arms; an individual document's legal effect must be assessed separately.
German word for coat of arms, applicable to several types of armiger.
German for the assumption or adoption of arms, not necessarily a grant.
German for the formal written description of a coat of arms, often supplied with a registration.
German for a written instrument recording or conferring arms.
German for an armorial book or compilation, not necessarily an official register.
German for a roll or register of arms, which may be privately maintained.
Two water containers suspended from a carrying yoke.
A pattern formed in paper manufacture useful for dating and identifying paper stocks.
A gently undulating line or edge used in divisions or figures.
A circular spoked object appearing in civic, craft and personal arms.
Of a pair of wings, shown back to back.
Wings spread so that both are clearly visible.
A canine heraldic charge shown in various attitudes.
The torse, usually comprising alternating twists of two tinctures.
A two-legged dragon-like creature in much English heraldic convention.
A fantastical beast with horns, whose artistic depiction varies.
Polish term associated with heraldic calls, proclamations or group designations.
